summary:
A.I.M.S. (Astronaut Integrity & Mission Support) is an ESP32-based wearable health-monitoring and mission-support platform developed for the NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026.

Combining physiological and motion sensors with an onboard REST API and a browser-based mission dashboard, A.I.M.S. collects, processes, visualizes and locally logs astronaut health indicators.

Its primary objective is continuous health-data harvesting and longitudinal monitoring to support research into the physiological effects of long-duration spaceflight. The platform currently supports heart-rate and SpO2 monitoring, motion and acceleration tracking, health alerts, routine checkups, mood logging and persistent data storage.

Designed with extensibility in mind, A.I.M.S. provides a foundation for future integration of immune biomarkers, additional cardiovascular measurements and radiation-monitoring instruments, including MOSFET dosimetry and CANS-related data.

The project aims to transform individual health readings into a persistent, structured record that can help astronauts and researchers understand physiological changes throughout a mission.
details:
A.I.M.S. – Astronaut Integrity & Mission Support

The Problem

Long-duration space missions expose astronauts to multiple physiological challenges, including cardiovascular changes, immune-system alterations, muscle and bone loss, sensorimotor disturbances, radiation exposure and behavioural health challenges.

These conditions can develop progressively. Individual readings or occasional health checkups may not provide enough information to understand how an astronaut's physiological condition changes throughout a mission.

A continuous, accessible and persistent health-data collection system can help address this gap.

Our Solution

A.I.M.S. is a wearable astronaut health-monitoring and mission-support platform developed using an ESP32 microcontroller and a standalone web dashboard.

The system is built around one primary objective: continuous health-data harvesting, structured logging and longitudinal monitoring.

The wearable collects physiological and motion-related information, processes measurements locally and makes the telemetry available through an API hosted directly on the ESP32.

A browser-based dashboard connects to this API and presents the collected information through health indicators, crew visualizations, event logs and mission-support interfaces.

Hardware Architecture

The current prototype consists of:

  • ESP32 DevKit – Main microcontroller, onboard processing, Wi-Fi communication and REST API hosting.
  • MPU6050 Accelerometer – Motion, acceleration and activity-related measurements.
  • MAX30102 IR Sensor – Optical heart-rate and SpO2 monitoring through photoplethysmography.
  • 0.96-inch I2C OLED Display – On-device health information and interactive checkups.

Implemented Features

Physiological Monitoring

  • Heart-rate monitoring.
  • SpO2 monitoring.
  • PPG sensor support.
  • Motion and activity tracking.
  • Acceleration and experimental force estimation.
  • Configurable abnormal-vital alerts.

Crew Health Support

  • Guided health checkups.
  • Mood check-ins.
  • Hydration reminders.
  • Exercise reminders.
  • Routine health reminders.
  • Health-event detection and logging.

Persistent Data Collection

The ESP32 uses LittleFS flash storage to maintain CSV records of:

  • Vital-sign measurements.
  • System and health events.
  • Mood assessments.
  • Reminder completion.
  • Health checkup results.

This provides a persistent history that can be used to compare measurements over time.

Mission Dashboard

The standalone HTML dashboard connects directly to the ESP32 through its native REST API.

It provides:

  • Live telemetry visualization.
  • Crew health status.
  • Astronaut injury-region visualization.
  • Mission event logs.
  • EVA safety simulation.
  • Communication-status visualization.
  • Emergency scenario demonstrations.

The dashboard also supports USB serial communication.

Research Alignment

A.I.M.S. is designed to complement research interests associated with NASA's ARCHeR program and the broader Spaceflight Standard Measures framework.

Its physiological monitoring and activity-recording architecture can support future research into:

  1. Immune-system changes through regular health assessments and future biomarker integration.
  2. Cardiovascular changes through heart-rate, PPG and oxygen-saturation records.
  3. Sensorimotor adaptation through motion and acceleration history.
  4. Gastrointestinal health through future nutrition and symptom-record integration.
  5. Musculoskeletal deconditioning through activity and exercise records.
  6. Radiation exposure through proposed integration of MOSFET dosimetry and CANS-related measurements.

These represent a combination of implemented capabilities and proposed research extensions. The prototype does not currently measure all six physiological areas directly.

Data Architecture

A key design decision is that the ESP32 hosts its own REST API.

The browser dashboard communicates directly with the wearable over Wi-Fi, avoiding the need for a separate backend server in the standard setup.

The architecture is:

Wearable Sensors → ESP32 Processing → Local Data Storage → Native REST API → Web Dashboard → Historical Health Visualization.

This approach is intended to support modular sensor integration and reduce dependence on external connectivity for local data retention.

NASA Data and Research Context

The team researched NASA astronaut-health research resources, including ARCHeR-related activity and well-being research, Spaceflight Standard Measures and relevant space-biology datasets.

These resources informed the project's research direction and the selection of health indicators and potential future integrations.

The current hardware demonstration is based on sensor telemetry and locally generated records; it does not claim to directly ingest NASA research datasets.

Future Development

Potential future extensions include:

  • Immune biomarker integration.
  • Sleep and circadian monitoring.
  • Expanded cardiovascular measurements.
  • Dedicated balance assessments.
  • Nutrition and gastrointestinal symptom tracking.
  • Muscle-strength and bone-density data integration.
  • MOSFET radiation dosimetry.
  • CANS-compatible neutron radiation records.
  • Multi-crew monitoring.
  • Advanced longitudinal analysis and predictive health models.

Impact

A.I.M.S. demonstrates a practical approach to integrating wearable hardware, embedded data processing, persistent storage and mission-oriented visualization.

By prioritizing continuous data acquisition over isolated readings, it aims to establish a foundation for better understanding astronaut health changes throughout long-duration space missions.

A.I.M.S. – Monitor continuously. Record intelligently. Understand astronaut health over time.
